title: Physical and mathematical models
subtitle: Four kinds of model, and how a differential equation becomes a program.

sections.title: Kinds of model
sections.body: Physical models are scaled or analogue versions of the real thing — static (a scale model of a building) or dynamic (a wind tunnel, a circuit that mimics a mechanical system). Mathematical models describe behaviour with equations — static (an algebraic relation such as Ohm’s law) or dynamic (differential equations in time). Computers make the dynamic mathematical model the workhorse.

questions.prompt: A differential equation describing how a tank level changes is a…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It relates rates of change to state.

sections.title: From a differential equation to a simulation
sections.body: Most dynamic models are of the form dy/dx = f(x, y). Euler’s method advances in small steps: yn+1 = yn + h·f(xn, yn). Runge–Kutta 4 uses four slopes per step and is far more accurate. For y′ = x + y, y(0) = 1 (exact y = 2eˣ − x − 1), at x = 1 with h = 0.1: Euler gives 3.18748, RK4 gives 3.43656, exact 3.43656.

worked.why: One Euler step from (0, 1) with h = 0.1 for y′ = x + y.

questions.prompt: Why is Euler’s method less accurate than RK4?

choices.text: It uses only the slope at the start of each step.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Step size is chosen by the user.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The error per step is O(h²) versus O(h⁵).

figures.caption: Figure 2.2.1 — Euler versus RK4
figures.note: Grey = exact; Euler lags behind; RK4 sits on top of it.

sections.title: Partial differential equations: heat flow
sections.body: When the state varies in space as well as time we have a PDE. The heat equation ut = α uxx is discretised on a grid: uiⁿ⁺¹ = uiⁿ + r(ui−1ⁿ − 2uiⁿ + ui+1ⁿ) with r = αΔt/Δx². The explicit scheme is stable only for r ≤ ½. A rod with ends held at 100 and 0 relaxes to the straight line between them: mid-rod temperature 49.997 after 400 steps (steady value 50).

questions.prompt: If r = αΔt/Δx² exceeds ½ in the explicit scheme…

choices.text: The solution becomes unstable and blows up.

figures.caption: Figure 2.3.1 — heat conduction in a rod
figures.note: Each curve is a later time; the last approaches a straight line.

sections.title: A physical model in the notebook: a damped oscillator
sections.body: SIMBLIP’s physics engine is itself a dynamic physical model solving Newton’s second law. A mass on a spring obeys m x″ + c x′ + k x = 0; the solution oscillates with angular frequency ω = √(k/m) and decays if c > 0. Press Simulate and compare the period with 2π√(m/k).

questions.prompt: Quadrupling the mass of a spring-mass system changes the period by a factor of…

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Period goes as the square root.

figures.caption: Figure 2.4.1 — Figure 2.4.1 — mass on a spring
figures.note: Press Simulate: m = 1 kg, k = 100 N/m, so T = 2π√(1/100) ≈ 0.63 s.

sections.title: Choosing a model’s level of detail
sections.body: A model should be as simple as the question allows. Include what affects the answer; ignore the rest, and state the assumptions (no air resistance, small angles, constant service rate). Validate by comparing with data; refine only where validation fails.

choices.text: So users know where it can and cannot be trusted.

problems.prompt: A pendulum model assumes small angles. Why, and what breaks for large angles?
problems.answer: For small θ, sin θ ≈ θ, so the equation becomes linear with period independent of amplitude. For large angles the true period grows with amplitude and the linear model underestimates it.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Physical vs mathematical, static vs dynamic.
  • ODEs: Euler is simple, RK4 accurate; PDEs: discretise space and time, watch stability.
